questions.q: A car rounds a flat, level bend at constant speed. What provides the centripetal force that keeps it on the curve?
options: The sideways static friction between the tyres and the road, directed inward toward the centre of the curve
A separate centripetal force generated by the engine and steering
The horizontal component of the normal force from the road surface
The forward driving force of the tyres pushing the car around the bend
questions.explanation: On a flat corner the only inward horizontal force available is sideways static friction, so friction is the centripetal force: friction = mv²/r. Option 1 is the misconception the episode warns against - centripetal force is never a new, separate force, it is the name for the net of the real forces resolved inward. On a flat road the normal force points straight up and has no horizontal component, so it cannot be it.

questions.q: On a frictionless banked track designed for one particular speed, a car travels SLOWER than the design speed. Which way does it tend to slide, and why?
options: Down the bank, inward, because the bank now provides more inward force than the smaller circle requires
Up the bank, outward, because the bank cannot provide enough inward force
Straight along the tangent, because friction has been removed
It stays perfectly on the design circle, because the banking angle fixes the path regardless of speed
questions.explanation: Going slower means less centripetal force is needed, but the fixed bank still supplies the design amount, so there is too much inward force and the car drifts down and inward. Sliding UP/outward is what happens when the car goes FASTER than the design speed (bank can't supply enough), so that option describes the opposite case.

questions.q: For a conical pendulum - a ball on a string of length L swept out at angle θ to the vertical - which quantity should you use as the radius r of the horizontal circle?
options: r = L sin θ, the horizontal distance from the ball to the central axis
r = L, the full string length
r = L cos θ, the vertical drop of the string
r = L tan θ, the string length scaled by the tangent
questions.explanation: The string is the slanted side of the cone; the radius is the horizontal distance from the ball across to the axis, which is L sin θ. Using r = L (the whole string length) is the classic trap the episode calls out - get it wrong and every subsequent number is wrong. cos θ gives the vertical height, not the horizontal radius.

questions.q: A ball is swung on a string in a vertical circle. Where is the string tension greatest, and why?
options: At the bottom, because the tension must both support the weight AND provide the centripetal force
At the top, because gravity and tension add together there
At the bottom, because the ball is moving fastest and speed alone sets the tension
It is the same everywhere, because the centripetal force mv²/r is constant around the loop
questions.explanation: At the bottom, tension points up (toward the centre) while weight points down (away from centre), so T − mg = mv²/r, giving T = mv²/r + mg, the largest value. At the top both forces point toward the centre and ADD, so tension only makes up the difference (T = mv²/r − mg) and is small - so 'top' is wrong. This is why a string is most likely to snap at the bottom.

questions.q: A bucket of water is swung fast in a vertical circle and the water does NOT fall out at the top. Which statement best explains why?
options: Gravity itself is providing the centripetal force, curving the water's path fast enough to keep pace with the bucket
The bucket base pushes up on the water hard enough to hold it against gravity
The centrifugal force on the water pushes it outward against the base
At high speed gravity effectively switches off, so nothing pulls the water down
questions.explanation: At the top the water is moving in a circle and needs a net downward (inward) force mv²/r; gravity supplies exactly this, curving the path so the water keeps pace with the bucket - it is effectively in free fall along a curved path. Nothing 'holds the water up': the base need not even push. Centrifugal force is a fictitious outward force, not the real explanation, and gravity never switches off.

questions.q: In UNIFORM circular motion, the centripetal force does no work. What does this tell you about the object's speed, and does the same reasoning hold in a VERTICAL circle?
options: Speed is constant in uniform circular motion; in a vertical circle the centripetal force still does no work, but the along-track component of gravity changes the speed
Speed is constant in both cases, because the centripetal force never does work anywhere
Speed changes in both cases, because a force always transfers energy
Speed is constant only in the vertical circle, where gravity keeps the energy topped up
questions.explanation: The centripetal force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does zero work everywhere - hence no energy transfer, constant kinetic energy, constant speed in uniform circular motion. In a vertical circle the centripetal force still does no work, but the component of GRAVITY along the direction of motion does (negative going up, positive coming down), trading KE and GPE, so the speed varies.

questions.q: Torque is τ = rF sin θ. According to the episode's 'reach, force, square-on' mnemonic, when is the turning effect of a fixed force on a fixed-length spanner at its MAXIMUM?
options: When the force is applied at 90° to the spanner, because sin 90° = 1
When the force is applied along the spanner, at 0°, because that pushes directly on the bolt
When the force is applied at 45°, halfway between along and across
When the force is applied at 180°, directly back along the spanner
questions.explanation: sin θ is largest (= 1) at θ = 90°, so pushing square-on to the spanner gives maximum torque - the 'square-on' part of reach, force, square-on. Pushing along the arm (θ = 0° or 180°) gives sin θ = 0 and no turning at all; you would only stretch or compress the spanner. 45° gives sin 45° ≈ 0.71, less than square-on.

questions.q: A bend of radius 50 m is banked at 30°. Assuming no friction, calculate the design speed - the single speed at which the banking alone holds a car on the circle. Take g = 9.8 and tan 30° = 0.577.
questions.given: r = 50 m, θ = 30° (tan 30° = 0.577), g = 9.8 m s⁻², frictionless banked track
working: Frictionless banked track: dividing N sin θ = mv²/r by N cos θ = mg gives tan θ = v²/(rg).
Rearrange for v²: v² = r g tan θ.
Note: mass never appears - it cancels - so the design speed is the same for a motorbike or a loaded truck.
questions.explanation: Using tan θ = v²/(rg) and rearranging gives v = √(rg tan θ) = √(50 × 9.8 × 0.577) ≈ 16.8 m s⁻¹. The mass cancels when the two component equations are divided, which is exactly why one banking angle works for all vehicles.

questions.q: A car of mass 1200 kg rounds a bend of radius 40 m banked at 20°. Assuming no friction is required, calculate the design speed of the bend. Take g = 9.8 and tan 20° = 0.364.
questions.given: m = 1200 kg, r = 40 m, θ = 20° (tan 20° = 0.364), g = 9.8 m s⁻², frictionless
working: Frictionless banked track: tan θ = v²/(rg), so v² = r g tan θ.
The mass 1200 kg is never used - it cancels out of the design-speed equation, so the answer is the same for any vehicle.
questions.explanation: v = √(rg tan θ) = √(40 × 9.8 × 0.364) = √143 ≈ 12 m s⁻¹. The given mass is a deliberate distractor: it cancels from tan θ = v²/(rg), so the design speed is mass-independent.

questions.q: A stone of mass 0.25 kg is swung in a vertical circle of radius 0.6 m. Calculate the minimum speed the stone can have at the TOP of the circle without the string going slack. Take g = 9.8.
questions.given: m = 0.25 kg, r = 0.6 m, g = 9.8 m s⁻²; minimum speed at the top means T = 0
working: At minimum speed the tension falls to zero, so gravity alone provides the centripetal force.
Set weight = centripetal force: mg = mv²/r; the mass cancels.
questions.explanation: At the top, T + mg = mv²/r; the slowest the stone can go is when T = 0, leaving mg = mv²/r, so v_min = √(gr) = √5.88 ≈ 2.4 m s⁻¹. Below this, gravity exceeds the required centripetal force, the stone leaves the circle and the string goes slack. Mass cancels, so v_min depends only on g and r.

questions.q: The same stone (m = 0.25 kg, r = 0.6 m) is moving at 5 m s⁻¹ at the BOTTOM of the vertical circle. Calculate the tension in the string there. Take g = 9.8.
questions.given: m = 0.25 kg, r = 0.6 m, v = 5 m s⁻¹ at the bottom, g = 9.8 m s⁻²
working: At the bottom, tension points up (toward the centre) and weight points down (away), so T − mg = mv²/r.
questions.explanation: At the bottom the tension must both provide the centripetal force and support the weight: T = mv²/r + mg = 10.42 + 2.45 ≈ 12.9 N. This is much larger than the tension at the top, which is why the string is most likely to snap at the bottom.

questions.q: A mechanic applies a force of 80 N to the end of a spanner 0.3 m long, at an angle of 60° to the spanner. Calculate the torque produced about the bolt. Take sin 60° = 0.866.
working: Torque: τ = r F sin θ.
Check via lever-arm reading: (F sin θ) × r = (80 × 0.866) × 0.3 = 69.3 × 0.3 ≈ 20.8 N m.
questions.explanation: τ = rF sin θ = 0.3 × 80 × 0.866 ≈ 20.8 N m. To maximise torque for the same force, apply it square-on at 90° (sin 90° = 1), giving 0.3 × 80 = 24 N m - the 'square-on' of reach, force, square-on.

questions.q: State the 'NET to the centre' method for solving any circular-motion problem, and name the four real forces you might draw on the free-body diagram.
keyPoints: Draw the free-body diagram with every REAL force as a labelled arrow - never add a separate 'centripetal force' arrow, because centripetal force IS the net of the real forces.
Resolve the forces and find the net component pointing toward the centre.
Set that net inward force equal to mv²/r (= mω²r).
The four real forces to consider: gravity (weight), tension, the normal force, and friction.
questions.explanation: Every scenario in the episode - flat corner, banked track, conical pendulum, vertical circle - is this one method in a different costume: name the real forces, resolve them toward the centre, set the inward net equal to mv²/r. The key conceptual point is that centripetal force is never an extra force, it is the name for the resolved net.

questions.q: Explain why the centripetal force does no work on an object in circular motion, and state the consequence for the object's speed. (This is a common 2-mark exam question.)
keyPoints: Work is done only by the component of a force along the direction of motion.
The centripetal force points toward the centre (along the radius); the velocity points along the tangent.
These are always perpendicular (90° apart), and a force at 90° to the displacement does zero work (cos 90° = 0).
Therefore the centripetal force does no work anywhere on the path.
Consequence: no work means no energy transfer, so kinetic energy - and therefore speed - stays constant in uniform circular motion.
A weak answer such as 'the force is used up keeping it in a circle' earns no marks.
questions.explanation: The two marks are for (1) stating the force is perpendicular to the velocity/displacement, and (2) concluding a perpendicular force does zero work. This is also the deep reason a satellite in circular orbit keeps constant speed with no engine - gravity is the centripetal force and does no work.
